bank-account.title: Opening a Bank Account
bank-account.subtitle: Bring your passport and ask how to open an account.
bank-account.culture: To open a bank account in China as a foreigner, you need your passport and often a local phone number. Major banks like ICBC and Bank of China are used to foreign customers, and a small initial deposit is required.

atm.title: At the ATM
atm.subtitle: Withdraw cash and handle common issues.
atm.culture: ATMs at major banks like Bank of China accept foreign cards, though daily limits apply. Guard your PIN, and if your card is swallowed (吞卡), contact the bank right away.

post-office.title: At the Post Office
post-office.subtitle: Buy stamps and mail a letter abroad.
post-office.culture: China Post (中国邮政) handles letters and parcels both domestically and abroad. Stamps can be bought at any post office, and international mail usually takes about a week or two.

visa-extension.title: Extending a Visa
visa-extension.subtitle: Ask what documents you need to extend your stay.
visa-extension.culture: Visa extensions for foreigners are handled at the Entry-Exit Administration (出入境管理局). Bring your passport, accommodation registration (住宿登记), and photos; processing usually takes several working days.

phone-topup.title: Topping Up Your Phone
phone-topup.subtitle: Add credit to your Chinese phone number.
phone-topup.culture: Phone credit (话费) in China can be topped up at convenience stores, online via WeChat or Alipay, or at carrier halls like China Mobile. You give your number, and a confirmation arrives by text.

police-station.title: At the Police Station
police-station.subtitle: Ask for help when something is lost.
police-station.culture: For help, foreigners can go to any local police station (派出所). Bring your passport, explain clearly, and keep the record number they give you for follow-up.

lost-id.title: Reporting a Lost ID
lost-id.subtitle: Cancel and reissue a lost ID document.
lost-id.culture: If you lose your ID or passport in China, report it to the police first and keep the receipt. For a lost passport, contact your embassy; for a lost resident ID, you can often get a temporary proof the same day.

print-shop.title: At the Print Shop
print-shop.subtitle: Print, copy, and scan documents.
print-shop.culture: Print shops (打印店) are common near universities and office areas in China. They offer printing, copying, scanning, and binding, and prices are usually cheap, around one yuan per black-and-white page.

rental-contract.title: Signing a Rental Contract
rental-contract.subtitle: Check the terms and sign the lease.
rental-contract.culture: A rental contract (租房合同) in China usually covers one year, with a deposit of one to two months. Read the terms carefully and keep a copy; agents often charge a fee equal to half a month's rent.

government-window.title: At a Government Service Hall
government-window.subtitle: Take a number and wait for your turn.
government-window.culture: Government service halls (政务服务中心) in China handle registration and permits. Take a number (取号) and wait for your turn, bring all required documents, and going early in the morning avoids long queues.
